chapter_theme: The order of kingship (அரசாட்சி முறை): an unlearned king is worse than Death; the king must follow and guard the way of austerity, test and punish false holy men and the faithless, protect the helpless, and take his sixth.
structure_note: 238 and 239 on the king's own learning and conduct; 240 to 242 on false wearers of holy garb; 243 to 245 on protection and the king's share; 246 and 247 on punishing drinkers and those who break their faith's rules.

238.reading: An unlearned king and Death are alike, but Death is much the better: the unlearned king, blind to dharma, says 'kill', while Death does not come near the good.
238.nuance: The comparison turns on discrimination: Death spares the good, the unlearned king doesn't.

239.reading: If a king does not every day look to the way of austerity in his land and keep to it himself, the land declines daily, folly sets in, and his wealth shrinks day by day.
239.nuance: நாள்தோறும் opens every line: the king's duty and the land's decline are both daily.

240.reading: What use is the holy garb to those who don't live by it? For those who do, it is the true garb; and if a strong king makes those who don't live by it do so, that leads to release.
240.nuance: It isn't clear whose release (வீடு) is meant: the false ascetics' once corrected, or the king's for correcting them.

241.reading: If those whose ignorance remains take up the tuft and sacred thread, the land withers and even a great king loses his standing; so, on reflection, it is good to cut off this showy thread and tuft.
241.nuance: The verse doesn't name who cuts them off; in a chapter on kingship, the king is implied.

242.reading: When those without knowledge put on matted hair, tuft and thread and act the part of the wise, it is good for the land that the king test them through the wise and bring them to knowledge.
242.nuance: The remedy is correction, not only punishment: the king tests them through the wise and makes knowledge arise.

243.reading: If the king, whose task is to protect cows, women, the virtuous and the holy ones the gods honour, fails to protect them, unending hell awaits him in the next world.
243.nuance: பாவை (lit. doll, image) is taken as women. The punishment falls on the king himself, after death.

244.reading: If you want release and wealth, keep to the path of dharma without lapse even in forgetfulness; and of all that is produced in the well-watered world, the king's share, as is declared, is one sixth.
244.nuance: The one-sixth share is the traditional royal tax. மறந்தும் means 'even by forgetting', that is, never. The two halves are loosely joined; திறந்தரு may be 'that gives strength' or 'excellent'.

245.reading: When the king guards the world well, worthy people follow the same path; but one who comes to seize the world, for others or for himself, has the evil nature of a pouncing tiger.
245.nuance: The second half is hard to construe: போந்திவ் வுலகைப் பிறர்க்கொள்ளத் தாங்கொள்ள may describe a king who lets others plunder or plunders himself. My reading is tentative.

246.reading: It is the king's duty to punish those deluded people who drink liquor instead of drinking the nectar taken by binding the breath, raising the fire and holding the moon's face.
246.nuance: கால் (breath), கனல் (fire) and சோமன் (the moon) are yogic terms: the breath held, the inner fire raised, and the nectar from the moon at the crown, traditionally. The verse sets the yogi's inner drink against toddy (தேறல்).

247.reading: Those who don't keep to the proper rules of their own faith suffer every punishment in the next life under the Agama law spoken by Siva; to punish them truly in this life is the king's duty.
247.nuance: The verse divides punishment between the two worlds: Siva's Agama in the next, the king in this. Each faith is judged by its own rules (தத்தம் சமயத் தகுதி), not by one.

links.note: Both say Death does not approach the good: the Kural that it does not advance on one who keeps from killing, Tirumular that it spares the good while the unlearned king kills.
Both tie the land's prosperity to the king's conduct: the Kural rain and harvest to just rule, Tirumular the land's decline to a king who neglects austerity.
Both condemn holy garb worn without the life it stands for; Tirumular adds that the king should force such men to live by it.
230 says the thread and tuft are only cotton and hair; 241 says they should be cut off from the ignorant who wear them, a ruler's remedy for what 230 diagnoses.
Both say the king who fails to guard harms cows and the virtuous; the Kural gives the cost to the land (less milk, forgotten books), Tirumular the cost to the king (hell).
Both make punishing wrongdoers a king's proper work, not a stain on him; Tirumular sets it beside punishment in the next world.

source_issues: 244: line 4 reads வேந்தனுககு, a misprint for வேந்தனுக்கு.
